Method

What CQC’s local authority assessments show about good adult social care

CQC has now assessed how almost every council in England meets its Care Act duties. This dashboard brings the 152 published reports together, so councils can see how they compare, what higher-scoring councils do differently, and who to learn from.

CQC scores each council from 1 to 4 on 9 quality statements: 1 means significant shortfalls, 2 some shortfalls, 3 a good standard and 4 an exceptional standard. The findings are CQC’s, quoted from its published reports. This site is intended to support learning between councils, not to rank them. Data as at 19 November 2026.

Councils assessed
152
Reports published May 2024 to November 2026
Overall ratings
Outstanding 4 · Good 91 · Requires improvement 54 · Inadequate 3
Highest scoring statement
Partnerships and communities
Average 2.9 out of 4; 122 of 152 councils scored 3 or 4 (good or exceptional)
Lowest scoring statement
Assessing needs
Average 2.2 out of 4; 117 of 152 councils scored 1 or 2 (significant or some shortfalls)
Main findings
Assessing needs
Higher-scoring councils prioritised people on waiting lists by risk

In all 8 councils that scored 1 (significant shortfalls), CQC described people waiting whom no one was reliably checking on. In all 31 councils that scored 3 or 4 (good or exceptional) and had a waiting list, CQC described people being prioritised by risk.

See what they did
Leadership
Councils that scored well on governance tended to score well elsewhere

Councils scoring 1 (significant shortfalls) on governance averaged 1.5 across the other eight quality statements. Those scoring 3 averaged 2.7, and those scoring 4 (exceptional) averaged 3.5. This shows an association, not cause and effect, and governance assessments draw partly on the same evidence.

Outstanding councils
What the four outstanding councils had in common

Barking and Dagenham, Camden, Kensington and Chelsea and Wigan all scored 4 on partnerships and communities and on governance. Wigan was the only council to score 4 on assessing needs.

Partnerships and communities
Partnership working had the highest scores

122 of 152 councils scored 3 or 4. The highest scorers included councils with joint leadership roles with health and integrated hospital discharge teams.

Theme: Working with people
Assessing needs

How councils assess the care and support needs of people and unpaid carers, and how quickly.

How councils scored
8
Score 2: 109
Score 3: 34
1

8 councils scored 1, 109 councils scored 2, 34 councils scored 3, 1 council scored 4. Average 2.2 out of 4. CQC’s scores: 1 means significant shortfalls, 2 some shortfalls, 3 a good standard and 4 an exceptional standard.

Key findings
What lower and higher scorers had in common

In all 8 councils that scored 1 (significant shortfalls), CQC described people waiting whom no one was reliably checking on. In Bedford, cases left open on the case system inflated waiting times, and the first check-in call came after six weeks. Salford’s teams kept their own lists, often outside the case system, and York’s teams each used their own risk ratings, so leaders had no overall view. In Hull the issue was reviews: the backlog reached 1,674 people, with a median wait of 193 days.

In all 31 councils that scored 3 or 4 (good or exceptional) and had a waiting list, CQC described people being prioritised by risk while they waited. Buckinghamshire used one risk tool in every frontline team, Hartlepool contacted everyone waiting each week, and Rotherham refreshed RAG-rated caseload data daily against a 30-day standard. Wigan, the only council to score 4, allocated two thirds of assessments on the day they arrived. A formal waiting well policy made little difference on its own: East Riding of Yorkshire had one and scored 1, and Warwickshire scored 3 without one.

How lower and higher scorers compared

Page numbers refer to each council’s CQC report. Select the examples link to see them below.

Area	What CQC found in lower-scoring councils	What higher-scoring councils did	Examples
Knowing who is waiting	Bedford’s waiting times were inflated by cases left open on its case system (p13). Salford’s teams kept their own lists, often outside the case system, so leaders could not say how long people waited (p15).	Rotherham refreshed RAG-rated caseload data daily, with a 30-day standard from first contact to sign-off (p10). Southend-on-Sea’s managers had a live dashboard of everyone waiting (p12).	See 4 examples
Contact while people wait	Bedford’s first check-in call came after six weeks (p15). Brighton and Hove could not see how often people on its lists were contacted (p11).	Hartlepool contacted everyone waiting every week (p12). Coventry called people regularly, gave them a waiting well pack and had set steps for anyone it could not reach (p12).	See 5 examples
Rating risk the same way	York’s teams each used their own risk ratings, so leaders had no view of risk across the whole list (p17). Southampton had a RAG tool, but teams used it inconsistently (p15).	Buckinghamshire used one risk tool in every frontline team (p15). Worcestershire triaged most referrals within one to three hours and aimed to respond to high-risk cases within 48 hours (p15).	See 5 examples
Reviews	Hull’s review backlog grew to 1,674 people, with a median wait of 193 days, after review staff were moved onto duty work (p6, p14).	Lambeth’s dedicated review teams cut the number of people waiting for a review by 48% in a year (p10 to 11). Wigan carried out 98.3% of reviews within six months of their due date (p16).	See 1 example
Unpaid carers	Bedford’s median wait for a carer’s assessment rose from 23 to 75 days in five months (p15).	Buckinghamshire assessed carers separately, with waits of around 18 days, and had a carers champion in every frontline team (p16).	See 1 example
Common shortfalls to check for
Waiting list figures leaders could not rely on, for example because cases were not closed on the system
A waiting well process that existed on paper but was not monitored
Teams rating risk in different ways, with no overall view for leaders
Carers added to the system only when the person they care for was assessed, so their waits were not counted
Review backlogs with no one checking on the people waiting

method.html.text:
Learning from CQC local authority assessments
National overview
Council profile
Quality statements
Method
Based on all 152 published CQC local authority assessment reports. Scores and findings were extracted using AI, and a sample was checked manually. How this was done
How this analysis was done

This dashboard is Edge Health’s independent analysis of published CQC local authority assessment reports. It is not an official CQC or government publication.

Coverage
The analysis uses all 152 local authority assessment reports CQC had published, from May 2024 to November 2026. Rutland is the only council whose report has not yet been published.
The councils include 4 rated outstanding (Barking and Dagenham, Camden, Kensington and Chelsea, and Wigan), 91 rated good, 54 rated requires improvement and 3 rated inadequate (Blackpool, East Riding of Yorkshire, and Salford).
Where CQC has replaced a report with a newer one, the earlier report has been used and flagged. This applies to Bath and North East Somerset and Wirral.
All figures on this site, including the ratings split and averages, are calculated from these 152 reports. Data is as at 19 November 2026.
Scores
Each report scores 9 quality statements from 1 to 4. CQC defines these as: 1, evidence shows significant shortfalls; 2, evidence shows some shortfalls; 3, evidence shows a good standard; 4, evidence shows an exceptional standard.
Scores were taken from the report text.
The overall percentage appears only in a chart near the start of each report, so it was read from there. In every report it matched the average of the 9 scores, as a percentage, rounded up.
Scores are categories rather than measurements. CQC itself combines the 9 scores into an overall percentage, and averages are used in the same way here, as a guide.
Ratings follow the bands shown in each report: inadequate up to 38%, requires improvement 39% to 62%, good 63% to 87% and outstanding 88% and above.
Findings and examples
For each quality statement, the relevant section of the reports was reviewed for the councils that scored lowest and highest, and for a selection of councils in between, to compare what CQC found.
Examples of practice come from one source: what CQC said councils did well, in CQC’s own words, with the page number. Only councils that scored 3 or 4 on a statement are used as examples for it.
Some examples were selected and tagged by Edge Health analysts. The rest were selected automatically from each report, favouring sentences with specific detail and leaving out general wording that CQC uses in many reports.
The same examples appear on the quality statement pages, as strengths on each council’s profile, and as suggestions for other councils.
For assessing needs, the main pattern was checked across every council that scored 1, 3 or 4.
Council profiles
Statements scoring 1 or 2 are shown as areas to improve, with sentences from the council’s report describing CQC’s concerns, examples from councils that scored higher, and councils in the same region to talk to.
Statements scoring 3 or 4 are shown as strengths, with what CQC said the council did well and councils in the same region that scored lower.
Sentences from CQC’s reports include both CQC’s own judgements and views CQC reported from people, staff and partners. CQC’s judgements are shown first where possible.
Councils are compared with others in the same region because regions are simple and widely understood. Statistical neighbour groups, such as CIPFA nearest neighbours, may be a closer comparison and could be added.
Use of AI
AI tools were used to extract scores from the 152 reports, to select sentences from each report describing what CQC found, and to help draft the summaries on this site.
The rules for what to select were reviewed and refined over several rounds.
A sample of the findings and examples was checked manually against the original reports.
All sentences shown as CQC’s findings are quoted from the reports, with page numbers and a link to each report on the CQC website, so you can check them against the source.
Limitations
A pattern shows what tends to go together, not what causes a score.
Councils differ in size, funding and local demand. Very small councils, such as the City of London and the Isles of Scilly, may not compare directly with large ones.
Reports describe each council at the time of its assessment, and CQC’s approach developed over the programme. Some councils will have changed since.
Findings selected automatically may occasionally be out of context. Each one gives the report page so you can check CQC’s full wording.
Source and licence

Quotations are taken from CQC local authority assessment reports, which are published by the Care Quality Commission. [Confirm licence and attribution wording before publishing.]

Get in touch

If you spot an error or would like to discuss the analysis, contact [Edge Health contact email].
